description: Museum-published exhibition-checklist facts and artist-authored comparison proposals. This file does not add graph nodes or edges, assert Lakehouse matches, attach object imagery, or represent museum approval.

source.title: World’s Fairs: Visions of Tomorrow — exhibition checklist (2025)

reviewProcess: Verify accession/edition and exact fields in the live institutional record with staff
Decide if each proposed comparison is a curatorial juxtaposition, not a metadata-proven graph edge
Request rights-cleared image and distribution permission; use text-only otherwise
Require editorial review and explicit published-source claim locators before any fictional scene is activated

candidates.title: Futurama (book page spread)
candidates.why: The exhibition checklist describes synchronized narration while visitors moved above an imagined city. Tests corporate authorship and the spectator's prescribed point of view.
candidates.publicEvidence: 1939 Futurama book spread; checklist describes conveyor seating and narrative soundtrack at General Motors pavilion.
candidates.question: What happens when a visitor can interrupt the voice that explains tomorrow?
candidates.limits: This record does not tell us what an individual fairgoer believed, nor prove that any Harlem Tours client attended the Futurama ride.

candidates.title: Harlem Invites You to Visit the New York World's Fair (leaflet)
candidates.creatorOrPublisher: Harlem “Hospitality” Tours, New York City, publisher
candidates.theme: Who is addressed by the future?
candidates.why: An invitation and organized itinerary for African American audiences offers a perspective on public access that differs from the corporate master-plan voice.
candidates.publicEvidence: The checklist states the advertisement offered tours, access to the Lido Recreation Center pool and endorsements including New York Urban League and Joe Louis.
candidates.question: Who is invited to a future, and who decides the route to reach it?
candidates.limits: Does not establish segregation within Futurama, actual attendance, visitor experience, or contact with General Motors representatives.

candidates.title: The Threatening Shadow (unexecuted maquette)
candidates.why: The museum reports that the proposed anti-authoritarian fair sculpture was rejected by organizers; a strong counterweight to technological optimism.
candidates.publicEvidence: The maquette is listed as never executed; checklist describes a proposed sculpture warning of authoritarian aggression, rejected by fair organizers.
candidates.question: What if the imagined future cannot make room for its own warning?
candidates.limits: The checklist supports rejection of the proposal, not the full decision process, organizers' private motives, or visitor reactions.

candidates.title: La Gloire du fer [The Glory of Iron] (sculpture)
candidates.why: Shows workers constructing the Eiffel Tower, giving the futures narrative an explicit account of labor and material infrastructure.
candidates.publicEvidence: Checklist identifies the sculpture, materials bronze/tin/brass and its commemoration of Eiffel Tower construction labor.
candidates.question: Can a monument celebrate progress without making its makers disappear?
candidates.limits: No proven connection to the 1917 On Munitions print; the comparison crosses separate moments and contexts.

candidates.title: Direct Route to New York World's Fair – Pennsylvania Railroad (poster)
candidates.creatorOrPublisher: Sascha A. Maurer, designer; Pennsylvania Railroad Company, publisher
candidates.why: Presents the technologies and commercial services that delivered fairgoers to the supposedly universal future.
candidates.publicEvidence: The checklist names the electrified railroad network and the publicity value of a direct route to the fair.
candidates.question: Who could reach tomorrow, and on whose terms?
candidates.limits: Advertising a route does not establish equitable affordability, ridership, or specific access outcomes.

candidates.title: Let's Go to the Fair and Futurama: New York World's Fair, 1964–1965 (pamphlet)
candidates.why: The museum describes a reprise of the Futurama concept at the 1964–65 fair, making recurrence and evolution of the narrated visitor journey visible.
candidates.publicEvidence: Checklist says the 1964–65 Futurama conveyed visitors using moving theater seats before a vehicle showroom; pamphlet is catalogued with two listed examples/credits.
candidates.question: Why does the future keep returning as a ride, and what changes between iterations?
candidates.limits: The checklist lists additional accession XC2017.01.2.311 for another illustrated example; confirm item-level record, edition and reproduction rights before use.
